catalog_quote: Stress is defined here as the syllable with the highest pitch. ... Like most Vanuatu languages, stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stress(es) falling on every other syllable counting backwards. /ˈa.wɛh/ ‘far away’ /ˈbe.ti/ ‘mat’ /beˈtul.ŋa/ ‘source (of river)’ /ˈna.liˈbau.wa/ ‘green sugarcane’ However, stress can also fall on the final syllable of multi-syllabic words. In this case, the rule for assigning secondary stress is the same. /naˈuh/ ‘rain’ /ˈnau.ti.ˈren/ ‘dawn, daylight’ ... In the above cases, the assignment of stress is likely to be due to the fact that these words are multi-morphemic. ... subject markers, such as the third person singular i=, typically do not carry stress ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three quoted passages (Appendix II §3.3 pp.728-730; ch.2 p.71; ch.1 p.17) are present verbatim at the stated locations in the held Brotchie 2009 text/PDF. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 PhD reference grammar (888 pp) with a phonology appendix, the sole descriptive work on Tirax per Glottolog 5.1 and per Crossref; no later grammar, JIPA illustration, or instrumental prosody study of Tirax was found. The coding (primary stress penultimate, secondary on alternate syllables leftward, with a pervasive lexical class of final-stressed words from historical final-vowel loss and unstressed proclitics/na-) faithfully reflects Brotchie's statements, including her own hedge that final-stress items are numerous ('just as many exceptions' for n(V)- nouns).
